Al-Tabari records many movements and events in chronological order, including developments in Iran before and after Islam up to his own time. He gives extensive detail on the Babak revolt, but he does not show the same care in checking reports that distinguished al-Baladhuri before him.↩︎

al-Mas‘udi became famous for three books: The Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems, printed in Cairo in 1346 AH and again in Cairo in 1958; The Book of Admonition and Revision, printed in Leiden in 1893; and Accounts of Time, Those Destroyed by Events, and the Wonders of Lands, printed in Cairo in 1938. His works generally combine historical events, descriptions of countries based on personal observation, explanations of theological schools, and accounts of other intellectual movements. But he does not pay much attention to checking the accuracy of events, observations, or transmitted reports.↩︎

Ibn al-Nadim is best known for al-Fihrist, printed in Leipzig in Flügel’s edition, 1871–1872, and in Cairo. al-Fihrist is rich in information from many branches of knowledge, especially the history of schools and beliefs. Historians and researchers have continued to rely on it up to the present day.↩︎

The Arab world began using modern movable-type printing in the early eighteenth century. It is well known that the deacon Abdallah Zakhir of Aleppo established the first press using Arabic type in the town of al-Shuwayr in Lebanon in 1748. But Arabic movable type had already been used in Europe since the sixteenth century, beginning in 1514, when Pope Leo X opened the first Arabic press in Italy for printing religious books. Ibn Sina’s Canon may have been the first work from the Arabic intellectual heritage printed in Europe, in Rome in 1593. After that, Arabic heritage works continued to be published in European cities and capitals such as London, Paris, Leiden, Leipzig, Göttingen, Rome, Vienna, Berlin, and St. Petersburg—now Leningrad—before Arab countries themselves were able to make broad use of this form of printing. From the mid-nineteenth century onward, it spread through the Arab world for printing old and new books, magazines, and newspapers. See Jurji Zaydan, History of Arabic Literature, Cairo, 1911, vol. 4, pp. 54–56.↩︎
